extracted.intended_audience: students, readers, and practitioners of political philosophy and constitutional government
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing what makes a form of government 'good' or 'best' for a people — focusing on representative government vs despotism, and on how institutions promote present welfare and future progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best government supplies what a people lack to advance
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best government for them is the one which tends most to give them that for want of which they can not advance, or advance only in a lame and lopsided manner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a proposed polity addresses the immediate impediments to social progress for that people. Consider whether the government supplies missing civic faculties (e.g., obedience, education, rule of law) required for the next stage. Examples/notes: 'leading-strings' (temporary paternal measures) may be admissible only as training to enable later self-government; they must be evaluated as transitional, not permanent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do no (or minimal) damage to existing goods when pursuing improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: In seeking the good which is needed, no damage, or as little as possible, be done to that already possessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging reforms or forms of government, weigh gains for progress against loss of existing liberties/qualities. Policy that attains short-term gains but destroys capacities needed for subsequent advances is disqualified. Historical cautionary examples: institutions that carried nations to a point then permanently arrested improvement (Egyptian hierarchy, paternal despotism of China).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forms that unfit people for subsequent stages of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of government which is most effectual for carrying a people through the next stage of progress will still be very improper for them if it does this in such a manner as to obstruct, or positively unfit them for, the step next beyond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether institutions cultivate faculties (mental liberty, individuality) necessary for later development. A regime that accomplishes immediate goals at the cost of citizens' capacity for future self-government should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government as ideally best form
rubrics_metrics.description: This ideally best form of government will be found in some one or other variety of the Representative System.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the representative system as the baseline ideal when judging constitutions: examine how sovereignty vested in the aggregate, periodic participation, and representation of interests contribute to both good administration and the moral/intellectual improvement of citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject 'good despotism' as a durable ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: A good despotism is an altogether false ideal... Evil for evil, a good despotism, in a country at all advanced in civilization, is more noxious than a bad one, for it is far more relaxing and enervating to the thoughts, feelings, and energies of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims that a benevolent absolute ruler can substitute for institutions: require demonstration that such a ruler can (a) be all-seeing and all-knowing in practice, (b) avoid creating citizen passivity, and (c) not hold liberties at mere sufferance. Consider empirical tendencies: despotism breeds civic passivity, stunts intellectual/moral development, and risks relapse into worse tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights secure only when individuals can stand up for them
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights and interests of every or any person are only secure from being disregarded when the person interested is himself able, and habitually disposed to stand up for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutions on whether they empower persons to defend their own interests (legal standing, political voice, mechanisms for redress). Measure real protection by the capacity and habit of self-protection, not by benevolent intentions of rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: General prosperity rises with the amount and variety of personal energies enlisted
rubrics_metrics.description: The general prosperity attains a greater height, and is more widely diffused, in proportion to the amount and variety of the personal energies enlisted in promoting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge governments by how widely they enlist citizens' energies in productive and public activities (economic initiative, civic engagement). Use historical comparative evidence (free states vs monarchical/oligarchical ones) as indicative: more distributed participation correlates with broader prosperity and better governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial extension of participation is the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The benefits of freedom, so far as they have hitherto been enjoyed, were obtained by the extension of its privileges to a part only of the community; and that a government in which they are extended impartially to all is a desideratum still unrealized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing reform or constitution proposals, examine inclusiveness of political participation (franchise, eligibility, representation). Exclusion leaves interests without guaranty and reduces incentives for self-improvement among excluded groups; partial extension has independent value but the ideal is universal participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government promotes development of active character
rubrics_metrics.description: A completely popular government is the only polity which can make out any claim to this character. It is pre-eminent... in promoting a better and higher form of national character... active rather than passive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether institutions cultivate energetic, self-helping citizens (intellectual, practical, moral). Prefer systems that reward exertion, public spiritedness, and provide practical outlets for civic talents rather than systems that encourage passivity and contented dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion and local self-management as checks on power
rubrics_metrics.description: He might allow such freedom of the press and of discussion as would enable a public opinion to form and express itself on national affairs. He might suffer local interests to be managed... by the people themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of freedoms and decentralized institutions (free press, local autonomy) that enable formation of independent public opinion. These are criteria for limiting arbitrary power and for enabling the transition from nominal to real constitutional rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary assumption of absolute power only to restore freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: I am far from condemning, in cases of extreme exigency, the assumption of absolute power in the form of a temporary dictatorship... but its acceptance, even for a time strictly limited, can only be excused... if the dictator employs the whole power he assumes in removing the obstacles which debar the nation from the enjoyment of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating emergency measures or temporary dictatorships, require clear criteria: temporariness, use of power to remove obstacles to self-government, and restitution of civil institutions. Otherwise such measures are illegitimate or dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that nominal freedoms held at sufferance are unstable
rubrics_metrics.description: The despotism, being thus chiefly nominal, would possess few of the advantages supposed to belong to absolute monarchy, while it would realize in a very imperfect degree those of a free government, since... they could never forget that they held it on sufferance, and by a concession which... might at any moment be resumed; that they were legally slaves, though of a prudent or indulgent master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the durability and psychological security of liberties: freedoms that can be withdrawn at ruler's will do not create genuine civic capacity. Prefer institutional guarantees (constitutional limits, rule of law) over contingent toleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political institutions should cultivate intellectual and moral faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the sphere of action of human beings is artificially circumscribed, their sentiments are narrowed and dwarfed in the same proportion... The food of feeling is action; even domestic affection lives upon voluntary good offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a government provides arenas for citizens to exercise judgment, responsibility, and public service. Institutions that limit civic action impair moral sensibilities and civic attachments; thus a good polity promotes avenues for voluntary public engagement.
